Online Network Design with Additive Delays
and Poisson Arrivals

Abstract

We study online service systems in which requests arrive at locations in a network. A service may open a facility and connect customers, buy a subtree linking them to a root, or send a mobile server to visit them. Combining requests can save opening, network, or travel costs, but each request pays its own waiting time. The objective is the sum of these spatial costs and individual delays.

We assume independent Poisson arrivals of known rates. The algorithms know how often requests occur, but observe them only upon arrival. We show that these rates suffice to make fixed spatial choices that compete with an offline optimum free to adapt to the realized input. We obtain long-run ratios of expectations below 27.24927.249 for facility location in finite metrics, 94.41594.415 for multi-root aggregation on trees, and 24.32624.326 for online service on trees. All three algorithms are deterministic; the multi-root algorithm also has polynomial-time preprocessing on rational inputs. The proofs connect rate-based spatial choices with lower bounds on unavoidable purchase, movement, and waiting costs. All main proofs are self-contained, and every guarantee includes the full cost of completing finite inputs.

1 Introduction

Consider a service provider receiving orders from customers across a region. An order can be handled as soon as it arrives, but doing so may require opening a depot, buying a connecting network, or sending a vehicle on a long trip for a single customer. Waiting allows nearby orders to share an opening or part of the route. The saving comes at a price: every customer left waiting incurs a delay cost. A good service policy must decide which orders to combine, where to serve them, and how long to wait before committing to service.

We study three versions of this choice. In facility location with delay, each service pays to open a facility and to connect every customer in its batch individually. Facilities are ephemeral: opening one again costs again. In multi-root aggregation, a service chooses one root and buys a connected subtree linking its customers to that root, sharing the cost of common edges. Roots may have nonuniform activation costs. In online service, a mobile server visits customers and retains its final position between services. In all three models, each request pays its own waiting time, and these payments are added to the spatial cost.

The distinction between choosing service times and choosing service locations is essential. If every client is assigned a facility or root in advance, its temporal decisions can exploit the aggregate demand assigned there. But the unrestricted offline optimum knows the entire realized sequence. It may send two occurrences at the same location to different facilities, or change the root of a batch when its realized composition changes. Thus a fixed assignment is an algorithmic restriction that needs to be justified against a comparator without that restriction. For a mobile server, even choosing a fixed home creates a restriction: returning there after every tour may pay for movement that an unrestricted trajectory avoids.

Known demand rates offer a way to make this choice before arrivals. We assume that each location generates an independent homogeneous Poisson process of known rate. The rates describe demand, but reveal no future arrival times. This stationary model isolates the question of whether statistical information can support constant guarantees despite the offline optimum’s freedom to adapt its spatial choices. The stochastic matching and rooted aggregation work of Mari, Pawłowski, Ren, and Sankowski [8, 9] provides the starting point: these papers report constant ratios of expected online and offline costs under independent arrivals. Here the additional difficulty is choosing facilities, roots, or a home for a mobile server. We ask whether the rates can justify these fixed spatial choices against an optimum that adapts to the realized input.

1.1 Our contributions

We compare expected online and offline costs over increasingly long horizons on a fixed finite instance. The offline optimum knows all realized arrivals and is free to choose every facility, root, or move. All three algorithms are deterministic and complete every finite input without being told when arrivals stop. Our main results are as follows.

  • •

    Facility location in finite metrics. We obtain a ratio below 27.24927.249, allowing nonuniform facility opening costs. The algorithm assigns each client location to a facility before arrivals begin. The guarantee holds even though the optimum can send different occurrences at the same location to different facilities. Thus a fixed assignment based on rates loses only a constant factor.

  • •

    Multi-root aggregation on trees. We obtain a ratio below 94.41594.415, with nonuniform root activation costs and polynomial-time preprocessing for rational inputs. The algorithm chooses one root for each client location, whereas the offline optimum may choose a new root for every batch. Both the root assignment and the service schedule are selected deterministically.

  • •

    Online service on trees. We obtain a ratio below 24.32624.326 when at least two sites have positive arrival rates. The server chooses a home using the rates and returns there after each tour. The comparator starts at the same specified location but can follow any trajectory. The result shows that this simple fixed-home structure costs only a constant factor, despite restricting where the online server waits between tours.

All three main proofs are given in this paper. The multi-root argument includes its own scheduling lemma for rooted forests, so no theorem from the prescribed-resource companion is needed. The numerical certificate for one spatial comparison is retained in the appendix.

1.2 Our techniques

The common idea is to use rates to decide where service should take place, then coordinate when requests use that service. The hard part is justifying a fixed spatial choice against an optimum that sees the future. The three models require different ways of measuring what that optimum must pay.

Facilities: balance distance against shared openings.

Nearby demand makes an expensive facility worthwhile only if enough requests can share its openings. We measure this tradeoff using local demand and distance, and select facilities that represent separated regions. The resulting assignment has a cost bound expressed through local client weights. For the lower bound, we retain requests whose nearby demand is not too crowded. Any offline batch must pay for these weights through its opening, its connections, or its requests’ waiting. The same weights therefore compare both schedules.

Roots: choose connected regions before scheduling.

On a tree, independent root choices can send neighboring clients in opposite directions. We instead assign connected regions to roots, using a specialization of the connected assignment method of Englert et al. [7]. An offline batch can be split among these regions at its original time: individual waits are preserved, and the extra spatial cost is bounded. Each region then becomes a rooted scheduling problem. A common cost certificate lets us choose one good assignment efficiently, before any arrivals are observed.

A mobile server: compare the two sides of each edge.

A home chosen from demand rates makes the algorithm easy to schedule, but the offline server need not return there. We choose the home so that no branch contains more than half the demand. Across every edge, there is then enough demand on both sides to force movement or waiting, regardless of where the offline server chooses to stay. We combine these edge comparisons without counting any request’s delay more than once. Coordinated tours from the home are bounded by the same quantity, giving the constant comparison.

1.3 Related work

Aggregation and delay frameworks.

Multi-level aggregation includes acknowledgment and joint replenishment on shallow trees. Bienkowski et al. [4] study online multi-level aggregation, and Buchbinder et al. [6] give depth-dependent guarantees for the deadline variant. Azar and Touitou’s frameworks [2, 3] connect aggregation, facility location, and other network design problems with delay or deadlines to common online constructions and offline primitives. These results concern adversarial inputs. Our statistical assumption and ratio-of-expectations criterion are different, and our constant bounds do not imply constant adversarial guarantees.

Facility location.

For linear delay, Bienkowski et al. [5] obtain an O⁡(log⁡m/log⁡log​m)O(\log m/\log\log m) guarantee in their one-sided model and a constant guarantee in a two-sided model with different connection and delay charges. We use ephemeral openings and one waiting cost per request. Our facility theorem allows arbitrary finite metrics and nonuniform opening costs; it compares a fixed assignment with an offline optimum free to change facilities between occurrences. The radius and space–time arguments are given in full.

Mobile service.

Online service with delay was introduced by Azar, Ganesh, Ge, and Panigrahi [1]. Azar and Touitou [2] developed a framework for metric optimization with delay or deadlines and obtained a randomized O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n) guarantee for service in general metrics. Touitou’s subsequent deterministic algorithm gives O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) [10]. These guarantees apply to adversarial arrivals and address a broader metric domain. Our constant bound uses known Poisson rates and the cut structure of trees; it does not give a constant guarantee for adversarial arrivals on arbitrary trees or for stochastic service in general metrics.

Information about arrival rates is also distinct from information about future delay functions. Touitou [11] studies nonclairvoyant service with delay. Here the delay function of each request is the known linear function; only the future arrival sequence is unknown. The algorithm’s additional information consists of stationary rates.

Stochastic arrivals and spatial projection.

Mari et al. [8, 9] study stochastic matching and rooted aggregation with independent arrival streams. Their aggregation work combines immediate service for infrequent demand with periodic service for frequent demand and motivates extensions to facility location. The connected 00-extension construction we specialize is due to Englert et al. [7]. The path-budget LP and synchronized-clock techniques used here are closely related. For the rooted forests needed in this paper, we give the full scheduling proof with an elementary scalar estimate; none of our main theorems invokes a result from that companion.

1.4 Organization

Section 2 gives the models and basic probability facts. Section 3 explains all three algorithms, their lower-bound ideas, and how the constants follow. These sections give the complete main story before the technical development. Section 4 records the probability tools. Sections 5, 6, and 7 give the full facility, multi-root, and tree-service proofs, respectively. Appendix A contains the connected-assignment analysis and its numerical certificate.

2 Models and basic Poisson facts

2.1 The three service models

The spatial instance and set of request types are finite. A type specifies a client location; distinct arrivals at that location are distinct requests. Request ii arrives at aia_{i} and is served at ti≥ait_{i}\geq a_{i}, incurring waiting cost ti−ait_{i}-a_{i}. In every model we minimize spatial cost plus the sum of these individual waiting costs. We write d⁡(u,v)d(u,v) for distance and w⁡(S)w(S) for the sum of edge costs in an edge set SS.

Facility location.

Possible clients and facilities lie in a finite metric. Facility ff has opening cost cf≥0c_{f}\geq 0. A service chooses a facility and a batch of pending requests, pays the opening cost once, and pays the distance to the facility separately for every request. The facility closes after the service. A later service pays another opening cost.

Multi-root aggregation.

Clients lie at vertices of a finite tree with nonnegative edge costs. There is a nonempty set of available roots, with activation cost cr≥0c_{r}\geq 0 for root rr. A service chooses a root and a connected subtree containing that root and its served clients. It pays the activation once and each edge of the subtree once. Later services purchase their networks again. Different batches may choose different roots, including in the offline optimum.

Online service.

A single server starts at a specified vertex s0s_{0} of a finite tree. Traversing an edge costs its length, and visiting a vertex serves all pending requests there for free. The server retains its position between services and may move proactively. The offline server starts at the same s0s_{0} and has no obligation to return to any home. Zero-length edges may be contracted.

All services and moves take zero time; there are no capacities. Arrivals at a service time are observed first, and simultaneous actions are processed in execution order. Splitting a batch into simultaneous services preserves additive waiting, though its spatial cost may change. This distinction will be useful for root assignments.

2.2 Arrivals and performance

Type xx follows a homogeneous Poisson process of known rate λx≥0\lambda_{x}\geq 0, independently of other types. Equivalently, its successive interarrival times are independent exponentials of mean 1/λx1/\lambda_{x} when the rate is positive. The algorithm knows the rates and spatial instance, but sees requests only upon arrival. Zero-rate types can be discarded; their locations remain available for spatial constructions and travel.

Let ITI_{T} contain the requests arriving in [0,T][0,T]. The algorithm receives no end-of-input signal and must eventually complete all requests. Its cost ALGT=ALG⁡(IT)\operatorname{ALG}_{T}=\operatorname{ALG}(I_{T}) includes all service, movement, and waiting needed after TT. The offline optimum OPTT\operatorname{OPT}_{T} completes the same input with full knowledge of the realized arrivals. For a fixed instance with positive optimal asymptotic cost, we use

RoE⁡(ALG)=lim supT→∞𝔼⁡[ALGT]𝔼⁡[OPTT].\operatorname{RoE}(\operatorname{ALG})=\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}_{T}]}{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}]}. (1)

This compares expected total costs, not expected samplewise ratios. We write OI​(1)O_{I}(1) for a finite constant depending on the instance but not on TT. Our estimates include completion before taking limits.

2.3 Basic Poisson calculations

A fixed interval of length pp contains λ​p\lambda p arrivals in expectation and is empty with probability e−λ​pe^{-\lambda p}. Counts in disjoint intervals are independent. Combining independent streams adds their rates; independently retaining each arrival with probability uu gives a Poisson stream of rate u​λu\lambda.

Conditional on a fixed number of arrivals in an interval, their unordered times are independent uniform points. Hence collecting rate-λ\lambda arrivals for a fixed period pp and serving at its end incurs expected waiting λ​p2/2\lambda p^{2}/2, or rate λ​p/2\lambda p/2 over repeated periods. This is the elementary waiting calculation used below. These facts concern intervals fixed independently of arrivals; we do not assume they hold for batches chosen after seeing the future. The more general identities needed for lower bounds are proved in Section 4.

3 How the three guarantees are obtained

The algorithms make their main spatial choices before requests arrive: an assignment to facilities, an assignment to roots, or a home for the server. This section explains why those restrictions are affordable. In each case we identify a quantity that bounds both the algorithm’s expected cost and the unrestricted optimum’s expected cost. The technical sections establish the exact constructions and estimates.

3.1 Facilities: choose where nearby demand should meet

Two nearby clients may benefit from sharing an expensive facility opening. Assigning each to its nearest facility can miss this saving; assigning everyone together can instead create excessive connection cost. Arrival rates help decide how much nearby demand is available to share an opening.

The spatial choice.

Around each facility we grow a radius until nearby demand is sufficient to balance its opening cost. Expensive facilities and sparse regions need larger radii. We select representatives in increasing order of these scales, suppressing facilities too close to one already selected. Each client is assigned to a representative that balances distance against the cost of supporting its openings. This uses only the rates, distances, and opening costs, not future requests.

The construction gives each client xx a weight αx\alpha_{x} measuring its local service scale. A nearby cheap facility makes this weight small; expensive service or sparse demand makes it larger. Let A=∑xλx​αxA=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}\alpha_{x}. The weights are chosen jointly, so they account for opportunities to share openings rather than charging every client for an independent facility.

When to serve.

After fixing the assignment, the requests assigned to a facility form one Poisson stream. Connections cost the same regardless of when those requests are served. Only openings and waiting need to be balanced. If the assigned rate is Λ\Lambda and the opening cost is cc, immediate service has opening cost rate c​Λc\Lambda. Service every pp time units has opening-plus-waiting rate at most

cp+Λ​p2.\frac{c}{p}+\frac{\Lambda p}{2}.

The algorithm chooses the cheaper mode and skips empty batches. The radius construction bounds its connections, openings, and waiting together by 19​A/419A/4 per unit time, apart from a finite completion cost.

Why the offline optimum must also pay.

It would be incorrect simply to charge αx\alpha_{x} for every arrival: a single offline opening could serve many nearby requests cheaply. The analysis therefore retains only requests whose neighborhoods in space and time are not too crowded. These retained requests carry a constant fraction of the total weight in expectation, by the Poisson arrival law. This selection is used only in the proof.

Now fix any offline batch. A retained request that is far from its facility, or waits a long time, pays for its weight through its own connection or waiting. The remaining retained requests are nearby and recently arrived. The crowding condition limits their combined weight, so the batch’s single opening pays for them. This is a comparison with every realized schedule, including one chosen with full knowledge of the input.

The resulting pair of bounds is

𝔼[ALGT]≤194AT+OI(1),𝔼[OPTT]≥2532e−3/2AT.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}_{T}]\leq\frac{19}{4}AT+O_{I}(1),\qquad\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}]\geq\frac{25}{32}e^{-3/2}AT.

Dividing gives the ratio below 27.24927.249. The facility count and the variation in opening costs enter through the same AA, and hence do not create extra factors. Theorem 5.2 proves the guarantee. The proof includes the radii, the assignment rule, the retention estimate, and the last clearing after arrivals stop.

3.2 Multiple roots: keep each assigned region connected

A tree service may choose a root afresh for every batch. A fixed assignment could be much more restrictive if nearby clients were sent toward different roots along overlapping paths. Connected regions avoid this problem: each client uses the path to the root of its own region, and different regions have disjoint edges.

Comparing spatial choices.

We first represent each root activation cost by an extra edge ending at that root’s terminal. Purchasing a path to the terminal then pays the activation exactly once. We specialize the connected assignment construction of Englert et al. [7] to partition this augmented tree into regions, one per terminal.

For any fixed offline service, split its requests by assigned root and serve the resulting batches at the original time. Every request keeps exactly the same waiting cost. The connected assignment bounds the increase in spatial cost, averaged over a finite distribution of partitions, by 313/8313/8. The same distribution works for every input and is chosen before arrivals. This step is where additive delay is essential: splitting a batch does not repeat its requests’ waits.

Scheduling one chosen forest.

Once the regions are fixed, every client has a prescribed root path. We schedule these paths using a rooted-forest lemma proved in this paper. Its LP distributes edge purchase costs and request waiting costs among simpler time scales, without charging either budget more than once. A direct one-resource argument supplies the lower bound: between consecutive arrivals, the schedule must either buy another service or pay enough waiting. Poisson gap probabilities turn this observation into an expected cost certificate.

The LP dual supplies service periods. We align them so that a longer period is an integer multiple of each shorter one. Requests due together share their root edges; empty queues buy nothing. Both the offline lower bound and the online upper bound are expressed through the same LP value. Their ratio gives a rooted-forest scheduling factor 1431/5931431/593. No result from the prescribed-resource companion is invoked for this step.

Selecting one assignment efficiently.

The spatial comparison initially averages over partitions, whereas our final algorithm must choose one. We do not search through all connected assignments. On a tree, compatible labels at vertices and edges describe connected root regions. A polynomial-size LP and a decomposition of its solution produce a polynomial-size list of assignments with the required averaged spatial bound.

Each candidate forest has a computable scheduling certificate. Choose the candidate with the smallest such value. Its value is no larger than the average, and its online cost is controlled by that same value. Thus we obtain one deterministic assignment from the known instance, rather than choosing a partition after seeing arrivals. Rational periods can also be selected in polynomial time.

The two losses have separate meanings: one pays for fixing the roots, and the other pays for online scheduling within those fixed regions. Together they give

3138⋅1431593<94.415.\frac{313}{8}\cdot\frac{1431}{593}<94.415.

Theorem 6.13 gives the full deterministic polynomial guarantee. Section 6.2 proves the temporal lemma, Section 6.5 proves the efficient selection, and Appendix A proves the spatial comparison, including its finite arithmetic certificate.

3.3 A mobile server: choose a balanced home

A mobile server carries its position from one service to the next. Repeatedly returning to a poorly chosen home can waste movement that the offline server avoids. Choosing the highest-rate vertex is not enough: a distant group of individually less frequent clients may have much greater combined demand.

We choose a rate-weighted centroid hh of the tree: every component remaining after its removal has at most half the total rate. The algorithm moves to hh initially and returns there after each tour. The offline comparator starts at the original specified position and retains complete freedom to move and wait elsewhere.

Coordinating the tours.

Starting from the home, we assign a service scale to each vertex by balancing the movement needed to reach it against the demand below it. Sparse demand favors serving without much extra waiting; frequent demand supports collecting a larger batch. The scales increase along paths away from home. Rounding them to aligned periods means that a tour visiting a distant due request can also serve due requests along its path.

At a tick, the server takes the union of paths to due nonempty queues, traverses that subtree, and returns home. Each shared edge is used at most once in each direction. Other pending requests encountered on the tour are served as well. Every request is served by its next own tick, so the policy also completes a finite input without an end signal.

A lower bound that does not force OPT to return home.

Remove an edge and consider its two sides. Serving demand on both sides eventually requires a crossing or waiting. The centroid choice ensures that demand in the branch away from home can be matched with enough demand outside it. The analysis extracts balanced two-site Poisson instances from these streams and projects the original trajectory onto the two sides of each edge.

One request can affect several edge comparisons, so adding their full delays would overcharge OPT. We allocate only fractions of its waiting to these comparisons and show that the total allocation is at most its actual waiting. Crossing costs add along physical edges. The projection therefore gives a valid lower bound even for a trajectory that never returns home. The random selections in this argument are analysis tools; the actual online algorithm is deterministic.

Let BB denote the sum of client rates weighted by their service scales. The tour analysis and the edge projections give, respectively,

𝔼⁡[ALGT]≤C0​B​T+OI​(1),𝔼⁡[OPTT]≥116​B​T,C0=1+14​(ln⁡2)2.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}_{T}]\leq C_{0}BT+O_{I}(1),\qquad\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}]\geq\frac{1}{16}BT,\qquad C_{0}=1+\frac{1}{4(\ln 2)^{2}}.

Thus the ratio is at most 16​C0<24.32616C_{0}<24.326. The finite completion term includes the initial move from s0s_{0} to hh. Theorem 7.8 gives the full result. Its proof first establishes the two-site comparison, then bounds the tours, and finally combines the edge projections without repeated charging.

What is common, and what is not.

In all three models, rates justify a fixed spatial policy by connecting its cost to a lower bound on unrestricted OPT. The lower bounds differ because an opening, a rooted purchase, and a persistent trajectory create different opportunities for sharing. We retain complete proofs of all three comparisons. Polynomial bit complexity is established for multi-root preprocessing; the facility and mobile constructions retain their stated finite, exact-real descriptions.

4 Probability tools for the proofs

The preceding sections described the algorithms and the comparisons behind their guarantees. We now give the complete technical arguments. This section collects the Poisson identities used to average the lower-bound constructions; subsequent sections prove the model-specific estimates. The insertion identity counts the contribution of a request whose weight depends on neighboring arrivals. It is an analysis tool, not information supplied to the online algorithms.

We write z+=max⁡{z,0}z_{+}=\max\{z,0\}, use 𝟏A\mathbf{1}_{A} for the indicator of an event, and let |J||J| denote the length of a measurable time set. Charging intervals are half-open. Nonnegative terms permit exchanges of sums, integrals, and expectations by Tonelli’s theorem.

4.1 Poisson identities used in the proofs

For a rate-λ\lambda process, the number N⁡(J)N(J) of arrivals in an interval JJ has distribution

Pr⁡(N⁡(J)=k)=e−λ​|J|​(λ​|J|)kk!,𝔼⁡[N⁡(J)]=Var⁡(N⁡(J))=λ​|J|.\Pr(N(J)=k)=e^{-\lambda|J|}\frac{(\lambda|J|)^{k}}{k!},\qquad\mathbb{E}[N(J)]=\operatorname{Var}(N(J))=\lambda|J|.

Counts in disjoint intervals are independent. Conditional on nn arrivals in a finite interval, their unordered times are nn independent uniform points in that interval. In particular, for a nonnegative deterministic function gg,

𝔼⁡[∑ai∈[0,T]g⁡(ai)]=λ​∫0Tg⁡(t)​𝑑t.\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a_{i}\in[0,T]}g(a_{i})\right]=\lambda\int_{0}^{T}g(t)\,dt. (2)

Conditioning on the count proves this identity: the conditional expectation is n​T−1​∫0Tg⁡(t)​𝑑tnT^{-1}\int_{0}^{T}g(t)\,dt, and 𝔼⁡[n]=λ​T\mathbb{E}[n]=\lambda T. We use it, for example, with g⁡(t)g(t) equal to the wait until the next deterministic clock tick. Nonnegative integrands also allow us to exchange sums, integrals, and expectations by Tonelli’s theorem.

For independent streams, superposition adds their rates. Conversely, independently assigning an arrival a mark jj with probability qjq_{j} produces independent Poisson streams of rates qj​λq_{j}\lambda. The generating function 𝔼⁡[∏jzjNj]=exp⁡(λ​|J|​∑jqj​(zj−1))\mathbb{E}[\prod_{j}z_{j}^{N_{j}}]=\exp(\lambda|J|\sum_{j}q_{j}(z_{j}-1)) factors into the generating functions of these independent counts. These statements apply to marks chosen independently for each occurrence; arbitrary routing based on the future need not preserve a Poisson law.

The void probability is Pr⁡(N⁡(J)=0)=e−λ​|J|\Pr(N(J)=0)=e^{-\lambda|J|}. It remains valid for a deterministic interval that depends on the instance parameters. We will not apply it to intervals selected by an offline schedule after observing arrivals. Instead, our lower bounds first establish an inequality for every realized schedule and then average a certificate whose counting regions are fixed independently of that schedule.

We also use the following extension of (2), in which the contribution of a distinguished arrival depends on the other arrivals. It is useful for the local facility certificates.

Lemma 4.1 (Poisson insertion).

Fix xx, and let ux​(a,J)u_{x}(a,J) be a nonnegative measurable quantity defined for a distinguished type-xx request at time aa and a finite multiset JJ of other requests. Then

5 Proof of the facility guarantee

A facility service combines a shared opening with an individual connection for every customer. It may be beneficial to send several nearby, infrequent client streams to one facility and share its openings; doing so also increases some connection distances. This couples the spatial assignment to the service frequency. The offline optimum can make that tradeoff anew for every realized batch, whereas we will choose one assignment using only the rates.

Idea and illustration.

Consider two client locations close to the same expensive facility. Analyzing them separately ignores the saving from their combined arrival rate. Assigning every client to its nearest facility can also miss a worthwhile shared opening. We therefore grow a radius according to nearby demand and the cost of an opening, rather than choosing an assignment from distances alone. Separated representatives give the algorithm’s facilities. A related radius at each client supplies a weight for the lower-bound proof.

The comparison with the optimum must account for congestion: arbitrarily many requests may be close to the same offline opening, so one opening cannot pay an unrestricted sum of their weights. We retain a subset with bounded local crowding and show that openings, connections, or individual waiting pay those weights. The same potential bounds the cost of our assignment. After the model, we construct the radii and assignment and analyze the online service periods, including completion. We then prove the offline certificate and combine the two estimates.

Notation.

Let (X∪F,d)(X\cup F,d) be a finite metric space, where XX contains possible request locations and F≠∅F\neq\varnothing contains possible facility locations. The sets may overlap. All distances are finite, and each facility ff has a finite opening cost cf≥0c_{f}\geq 0. Nothing requires opening costs to be uniform. Several service events at one time are allowed, but each has its own opening and delay charge. There is no capacity constraint or travel time.

The total cost is the sum over service events. The offline optimum may choose different facilities for different occurrences of the same type. The algorithm knows the metric, all opening costs, and all arrival rates.

6 Proof of the multi-root guarantee

Fixed-root aggregation prescribes one root path for each client. Here a service instead chooses a root from a given collection. A client near several roots may be served from one root in one batch and another in the next. This spatial freedom belongs to the offline optimum as well as to the original online problem, so choosing a fixed root for each client requires a proof.

Idea and illustration.

Imagine two depots at the ends of a tree path. Assigning clients independently to depots may send neighboring clients in opposite directions, making a single offline service expensive to reproduce. We use a tree specialization of the connected 00-extension construction of Englert et al. [7] to assign connected regions to roots. Once a region is fixed, every client in it has one prescribed path to its root. A service of the free-root optimum can be split at its original time according to these regions. Every request keeps the same wait; only the spatial cost can increase. A connected terminal assignment bounds that increase in expectation, uniformly for every fixed input.

There are three steps. We express activation costs as pendant edges of a tree. We then apply this connected assignment construction and compare the restricted and unrestricted offline optima. Finally, the rooted-forest lemma schedules the resulting fixed paths. The finite construction chooses an assignment once, before arrivals. Section 6.5 replaces its enumeration by a polynomial local-marginal LP and deterministic support selection.

6.1 The model and activation costs

Notation.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a finite tree with nonnegative edge costs, RR a nonempty set of static facility/root locations, and cr≥0c_{r}\geq 0 their activation costs. Each positive-rate client vertex xx has independent Poisson arrivals of known rate λx\lambda_{x}. A service chooses a root rr, a connected subtree SS containing rr and its served requests, and a time tt. Its cost is

cr+w⁡(S)+∑i​ served(t−ai).c_{r}+w(S)+\sum_{i\text{ served}}(t-a_{i}).

For every client location xx, define its singleton spatial cost

sx=minr∈R⁡{cr+d𝒯​(r,x)}.s_{x}=\min_{r\in R}\{c_{r}+d_{\mathcal{T}}(r,x)\}.

Use the completion and expectation-ratio convention of Section 2. The comparator OPTfree\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm free} may choose a different root for every service. A sampled assignment ff is included in the online expectation only.

For each rr, attach a new terminal r+r^{+} to rr by a pendant edge of length crc_{r}. A rooted service is now a connected network containing its selected terminal r+r^{+}. A nonempty service for ordinary client vertices includes this pendant edge and pays the activation exactly once. More precisely, for every nonempty client set AA,

w⁡(hullT^⁡(r+,A))=cr+w⁡(hull𝒯⁡(r,A)).w\bigl(\operatorname{hull}_{\widehat{T}}(r^{+},A)\bigr)=c_{r}+w\bigl(\operatorname{hull}_{\mathcal{T}}(r,A)\bigr).

Thus activation is paid exactly once in each nonempty rooted service. Contract zero-length edges, merge co-located terminals, and superpose co-located client streams. These operations preserve every schedule’s cost. Serve zero-singleton-cost types immediately for free and remove them. Deleting those occurrences from any schedule and adding them back as free immediate services proves that OPT\operatorname{OPT} is unchanged. If no type remains, both costs are zero. Otherwise let KK be the remaining terminals. A contracted terminal can be translated back to any original root in its zero-distance, zero-activation class.

6.2 Scheduling a rooted forest

Once every client has a prescribed root, the spatial choice disappears, but the service clocks still have to share common edges. We establish the scheduling statement needed below, including its offline certificate and polynomial construction. All arguments in this subsection are local; no scheduling theorem or numerical certificate from the companion manuscript is used.

Notation and the certificate.

Let FF be a finite rooted forest with positive rational edge costs wew_{e}. A positive-rate type ii occurs at a vertex in one component, has rational Poisson rate λi>0\lambda_{i}>0, and requires the path PiP_{i} to that component’s root. Zero-length edges are contracted, zero-rate types are omitted, and types with empty paths are served immediately for free. Unused edges may be removed. A service buys the union of the paths of its served requests and pays their individual waiting times. Unions in different components can be purchased simultaneously as separate rooted services, without an extra event fee. Thus this description preserves the original rooted-forest cost exactly.

If no type remains, the algorithm does nothing and both costs are zero. Otherwise let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the set of remaining types and put

Ci=w⁡(Pi),Γ=∑iλi,λmin=mini⁡λi,M=∑iλi​Ci.C_{i}=w(P_{i}),\qquad\Gamma=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i},\qquad\lambda_{\min}=\min_{i}\lambda_{i},\qquad M=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}C_{i}.

Fix the rational constants

∑e∈Pi,aδi​e​aa\displaystyle\sum_{e\in P_{i},a}\frac{\delta_{iea}}{a} ≤1,\displaystyle\leq 1, δi​e​a\displaystyle\delta_{iea} ≤ce​a,\displaystyle\leq c_{ea},
a∑i:e∈Piλiδi​e​a\displaystyle a\sum_{i:e\in P_{i}}\lambda_{i}\delta_{iea} ≤β​ce​a,\displaystyle\leq\beta c_{ea}, ∑ace​a\displaystyle\sum_{a}c_{ea} ≤we.\displaystyle\leq w_{e}.

The first constraint divides a request’s waiting budget among the edges and scales charged to it. The last constraint divides each edge purchase among scales. The two middle constraints control the size and mean load of the scalar problems used to certify the offline cost.

6.2.1 An elementary offline certificate

We begin with one purchase of cost one and unit waiting cost. Let JHJ_{H} be a rate-uu Poisson input on [0,H][0,H], and let Ou​(H)O_{u}(H) be its unrestricted offline cost, including completion.

Lemma 6.1 (A gap certificate).

For every u,H≥0u,H\geq 0,

𝔼⁡[Ou​(H)]≥(1−e−u)​H.\mathbb{E}[O_{u}(H)]\geq(1-e^{-u})H.

Extend the Poisson process to H+1H+1 for the analysis. Charge each arrival in [0,H][0,H] the smaller of one and its gap to the next arrival of this extended process, using charge one if there is no later arrival. Consider any batch of any completing schedule. Its latest arrival has charge at most one, paid by the batch’s purchase. For every other arrival in that batch, the next arrival of the full process occurs no later than the batch’s latest arrival, hence no later than its service. Its gap charge is therefore at most its own waiting. Summing over batches proves a pathwise lower bound, for every realization of the extension. This argument does not require batches to consist of consecutive arrivals.

At a distinguished arrival at time a≤Ha\leq H, the probability of no arrival in (a,a+t](a,a+t] is e−u​te^{-ut} for 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1. These intervals lie inside [0,H+1][0,H+1], so the expected charge is ∫01e−u​t​𝑑t\int_{0}^{1}e^{-ut}\,dt. The Poisson insertion identity, or conditioning on a distinguished arrival and integrating its time, therefore gives total expected charge u​H​∫01e−u​t​𝑑t=(1−e−u)​HuH\int_{0}^{1}e^{-ut}\,dt=(1-e^{-u})H. The zero-rate case is immediate. ∎

All preprocessing below uses the known forest and rates. Let BB be their total binary encoding length. The primal and dual LPs therefore have polynomially many rational variables and constraints, and rational linear programming supplies optimal solutions of polynomial encoding length in polynomial time.

Theorem 6.6 (Independent rooted-forest scheduling).

For every nontrivial rational rooted-forest instance, the certificate L∗L^{*} in (5) is positive and satisfies, for all T≥0T\geq 0,

𝔼⁡[OPTT]≥κ​L∗​T.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}]\geq\kappa L^{*}T.

6.3 Choosing connected root regions

A terminal retraction f:V⁡(T^)→Kf:V(\widehat{T})\to K fixes every terminal. We require each fiber to be connected, so that the path from a client to its assigned terminal stays inside one region. We obtain these regions by specializing the growing construction of Englert et al. [7, Section 4, Algorithm 1] to the tree. The following comparison is uniform over the offline service and its client set.

Theorem 6.7 (Connected terminal assignment).

There is a finitely supported distribution of connected terminal retractions such that every connected service subtree SS containing a terminal and every client set A⊆V⁡(S)A\subseteq V(S) satisfy

𝔼f[∑r∈Kw(⋃x∈A:f⁡(x)=rPT^(x,r))]≤3138w(S).\mathbb{E}_{f}\left[\sum_{r\in K}w\!\left(\bigcup_{x\in A:f(x)=r}P_{\widehat{T}}(x,r)\right)\right]\leq\frac{313}{8}w(S).

Consequently, for every finite input, 𝔼f​[OPTf⁡(I)]≤(313/8)​OPTfree⁡(I)\mathbb{E}_{f}[\operatorname{OPT}_{f}(I)]\leq(313/8)\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm free}(I).

Proof.

Appendix A gives this tree specialization with a finite mixture of quadrupling scales and proves the service inequality. Split each free-root offline batch by assigned terminal at its original service time. The displayed inequality controls its expected spatial cost, while every occurrence keeps the same waiting time. Taking the infimum over original schedules proves the second claim. ∎

The construction freezes assigned vertices and attaches each new connected component to one already assigned neighbor. Its labels never change. A random initial scale lets the analysis charge the first and last endpoint assignments jointly. The distribution is chosen once from the spatial instance, before any requests arrive.

6.4 From connected regions to an online algorithm

Fix a connected retraction ff produced by Theorem 6.7. For each positive-rate client type xx, define its required root path

Rxf=PT^​(x,f⁡(x)),Cxf=w⁡(Rxf).R_{x}^{f}=P_{\widehat{T}}(x,f(x)),\qquad C_{x}^{f}=w(R_{x}^{f}). (6)

Every such path lies in the connected fiber f−1​(f​(x))f^{-1}(f(x)), because a connected subset of a tree contains the unique path between any two of its vertices. If f⁡(x)≠f⁡(y)f(x)\neq f(y), the two paths in (6) are edge-disjoint. The pendant edge of a terminal belongs to every nonempty path assigned to that terminal, so purchasing a union of paths pays its activation cost exactly once.

Delete every edge whose endpoints have different labels under ff. The resulting forest has one component for each nonempty fiber, rooted at its terminal: connectedness makes the fiber a tree, and a second terminal cannot lie in it because terminals keep their own labels. Remove components and branches with no positive-rate clients. Denote the remaining rooted forest by FfF_{f}.

Lemma 6.8 (Exact rooted-forest reduction).

For every finite input II and every connected terminal retraction ff, the rooted-forest optimum on FfF_{f} equals OPTf⁡(I)\operatorname{OPT}_{f}(I), the multi-root optimum restricted to ff.

Proof.

Trim each ff-restricted service to the union of its clients’ paths to their assigned terminal. This is a feasible purchase in FfF_{f} with no greater cost. Conversely, split any forest purchase by component at its original service time. Each nonempty path union is connected to its assigned terminal and translates back into a valid rooted service. Components have disjoint edges, and the pendant activation edge is paid exactly once for each such service. Zero-cost contracted activation edges add nothing. Thus splitting preserves both spatial cost and waiting, proving equality. ∎

For each assignment, apply Theorem 6.6. Write Lf∗L_{f}^{*} for the rooted-forest LP value and BfB_{f} for the completion constant of its finite-preprocessing policy. The preceding exact reduction gives

𝔼I​[ALGf⁡(IT)]≤KF​Lf∗​T+Bf,𝔼I​[OPTf⁡(IT)]≥κ​Lf∗​T.\mathbb{E}_{I}[\operatorname{ALG}_{f}(I_{T})]\leq K_{F}L_{f}^{*}T+B_{f},\qquad\mathbb{E}_{I}[\operatorname{OPT}_{f}(I_{T})]\geq\kappa L_{f}^{*}T.

At each tick, split the due requests by assigned terminal and buy the union of their assigned paths as one rooted service per terminal. Connected fibers make these path unions edge-disjoint, so the forest purchase cost is reproduced exactly.

For rational costs and rates, the algorithm with one assignment sampled before arrivals satisfies

𝔼f,I​[ALGf⁡(IT)]≤3138​CF​𝔼I​[OPTfree⁡(IT)]+𝔼f​[Bf].\mathbb{E}_{f,I}[\operatorname{ALG}_{f}(I_{T})]\leq\frac{313}{8}C_{F}\,\mathbb{E}_{I}[\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm free}(I_{T})]+\mathbb{E}_{f}[B_{f}].

Combine the fixed-assignment inequalities with Theorem 6.7. There are finitely many assignments, each with finite periods, so 𝔼f​[Bf]\mathbb{E}_{f}[B_{f}] is finite. On the nonfree instance Lf∗>0L_{f}^{*}>0 for every assignment. The exhaustive selection in this theorem is finite, without a polynomial running-time assertion. The next section replaces it by a polynomial construction and uses the rational-period forest policy with the same competitive factor.

Assume binary-encoded rational tree lengths, root activation costs, and positive arrival rates. Zero-length contractions and free types are handled as in Section 6. Lemma 6.10 (Local characterization).

A labeling f:V→𝒦f:V\to\mathcal{K} fixing terminals is a connected terminal retraction if and only if every edge satisfies (7).

For a connected retraction, an edge between distinct fibers separates their terminals: otherwise the path from an endpoint to its own terminal would cross the edge and enter the other fiber. Thus unequal labels lie on the specified opposite sides.

Hence each fiber contains its terminal and is connected. ∎

6.5.1 An explicit polynomial-support decomposition

Lemma 6.12.

Any rational point satisfying (8)–(10) can be decomposed in polynomial time into at most n​k+(n−1)​k2nk+(n-1)k^{2} connected terminal retractions with nonnegative rational weights summing to one and exactly the given vertex and edge marginals.

Proof.

Keep residual marginals initially equal to x,yx,y. At each step they have a common total mass m>0m>0 at every vertex, obey consistency, and retain all forbidden zeros. Choose any positive label at oo. Proceed down the tree. If parent uu has chosen label aa, its positive residual xu,ax_{u,a} is the sum of row (a,⋅)(a,\cdot) at each child edge. Choose any positive entry yu​v,a,by_{uv,a,b} in that row and give vv label bb. Column consistency makes the selected xv,bx_{v,b} positive as well.

The resulting labeling fixes terminals and uses only allowed pairs, so it is connected by Lemma 6.10. Let ζ>0\zeta>0 be the smallest selected vertex or edge entry. Record this labeling with weight ζ\zeta, and subtract ζ\zeta from all its selected vertex and edge entries.

Nonnegativity is preserved. Each selected vertex entry and each corresponding selected row or column decrease by the same ζ\zeta, so consistency remains true, with common mass m−ζm-\zeta. At least one positive entry vanishes; none can reappear. Consequently there are at most as many iterations as initial vertex and edge coordinates. At zero common mass every residual entry is zero, proving exact reconstruction and that the recorded weights sum to one.

The arithmetic is polynomial. All residual values are differences of initial rational entries and previous subtraction weights; a common denominator given by the product of their initial denominators has polynomial bit length. The number of iterations is polynomial. ∎

The residual need not satisfy (11); only the original point needs those constraints. Its exactly reconstructed mixture therefore satisfies the required expected stretch. Individual support assignments need not satisfy the edgewise bound separately.

The O⁡(n​k2)O(nk^{2}) bound is the size of the marginal LP, not a bound on the full running time. Polynomiality is in the binary input length and is not strong polynomiality. The support assignments need not each obey the edgewise stretch constraints. Their mixture does, and the smallest forest certificate is what permits deterministic selection.

7 Proof of the tree-service guarantee

In online service, the spatial decision is a trajectory. A server serves pending requests by visiting their locations and retains its final position for the next service. This distinguishes it from a network that must be bought again at every event. In particular, a lower bound based only on distance from a designated root need not hold for a server that stays near the current demand.

Idea and illustration.

Consider two sites separated by a long edge. If only the far site receives requests, the server can move there once and stay. A policy forced to return home after every service would repeatedly pay an expense the optimum avoids. If both sites receive requests, however, avoiding a crossing leaves demand on one side waiting. The rates on both sides, rather than demand on just the far side, are therefore the appropriate basis for a lower bound.

On a tree we choose a rate-weighted centroid as the online home: each branch contains at most half the total rate. This ensures enough demand outside a branch to compare with its native stream. Independent marks assign each occurrence at most one auxiliary target. A second thinning distributes its waiting budget over one two-site problem per edge. A telescoping sum pays for all these projections, even though the offline trajectory need not return home.

7.1 The mobile-service model

Notation.

Let 𝒯=(V,E)\mathcal{T}=(V,E) be a finite tree with positive edge lengths ℓe\ell_{e}. Zero-length edges can be contracted. A server starts at a specified vertex s0s_{0}. A move from uu to vv costs d⁡(u,v)d(u,v) and takes zero time; intermediate vertices on the unique path are visited. A visit serves all pending requests at that vertex at no additional service fee. Requests at the server’s current vertex are served immediately. The server may move without a pending request, and the offline comparator may do so proactively.

For every vertex vv, an independent homogeneous Poisson process of known rate λv≥0\lambda_{v}\geq 0 generates requests. A request ii arrives at vertex viv_{i} at time aia_{i}. If the server first serves it at ti≥ait_{i}\geq a_{i}, its delay cost is ti−ait_{i}-a_{i}. The schedule’s cost is total movement plus ∑i(ti−ai)\sum_{i}(t_{i}-a_{i}). Requests are distinguishable even when several occur at the same vertex. The algorithm sees arrivals as they happen and never sees future arrivals.

Let ITI_{T} contain arrivals in [0,T][0,T], and let ALGT\operatorname{ALG}_{T} be the complete cost of our algorithm on this finite input. It runs without an end-of-input signal and must eventually clear every request; movements and waiting after TT needed to do so are included. The offline optimum OPTT\operatorname{OPT}_{T} knows ITI_{T}, may choose any feasible trajectory, and is not required to return to any fixed point. We prove an inequality of the form

𝔼⁡[ALGT]≤C​𝔼​[OPTT]+K⁡(𝒯,λ,s0),\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}_{T}]\leq C\,\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}]+K(\mathcal{T},\lambda,s_{0}), (13)

where KK is finite and independent of TT. For an instance with positive optimal rate, this implies the long-run ratio of expectations lim supT→∞𝔼⁡[ALGT]/𝔼⁡[OPTT]≤C\limsup_{T\to\infty}\,\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}_{T}]/\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}]\leq C. We do not replace it by the expectation of a samplewise ratio.

At a common time, arrivals are observed before service actions, and simultaneous moves are processed in execution order. Charging intervals are half-open: an action at the left endpoint belongs to that interval, and one at the right endpoint belongs to the next.

7.2 A two-site tool for the tree lower bound

Consider two sites at distance w>0w>0. Each request has waiting coefficient ρ>0\rho>0. The online and offline servers start at the same specified endpoint. While at one endpoint, serve arrivals there immediately. Wait until the total weighted waiting accumulated by the pending requests at the opposite endpoint reaches ww, then cross and clear all of them. An empty queue triggers no action.

Lemma 7.1.

For every finite request input, the threshold-crossing policy completes the input without an end signal and satisfies

ALG⁡(I)≤4​OPT⁡(I).\operatorname{ALG}(I)\leq 4\operatorname{OPT}(I).

The assertion permits arbitrary arrival times and does not require a Poisson input.

Proof.

Call the interval from one online crossing to the next a phase, with the first phase starting at time zero. At the beginning of every phase the opposite queue is empty. Every completed phase incurs movement ww and weighted waiting ww, so nn online crossings cost exactly 2​n​w2nw. If a finite input leaves a nonempty opposite queue, its waiting grows until the threshold is reached. Thus every pending request is eventually served, and there are only finitely many completed phases.

The first phase alone forces an offline payment of at least ww. If the offline trajectory crosses in this phase, charge a crossing. Otherwise it stays at the common initial endpoint, so the requests in the online opposite queue incur at least the entire online phase’s weighted waiting, namely ww.

Pair the remaining phases as (2,3),(4,5),…(2,3),(4,5),\ldots. In each complete pair, either the offline trajectory crosses, paying at least ww, or it stays at one endpoint throughout the pair. The two online opposite queues are at different endpoints. One phase’s opposite requests are therefore unvisited throughout their phase and incur at least its weighted waiting ww. All charging intervals are half-open. A crossing at a right endpoint belongs to the next interval; if it is the first visit serving the preceding requests, those requests have already incurred the claimed waiting. Movement charges use disjoint time intervals, and delay charges use disjoint sets of requests classified by their online arrival phase. They therefore do not reuse either cost account.

For n≥1n\geq 1, this gives OPT⁡(I)≥⌈n/2⌉​w\operatorname{OPT}(I)\geq\lceil n/2\rceil w. Consequently 2​n​w≤4​OPT⁡(I)2nw\leq 4\operatorname{OPT}(I). The case n=0n=0 has zero online cost. All intervals, movements, and waiting used here may extend beyond the arrival horizon, as required by the completion convention. ∎

If the two initial endpoints were allowed to differ, pairing phases from the first would still give ALG≤4​OPT+2​w\operatorname{ALG}\leq 4\operatorname{OPT}+2w. We use the stronger same-initial-endpoint statement: each virtual cut inherits its initial side from the given original position s0s_{0}. This fixes no home or subsequent trajectory for the offline server.

Write

g⁡(a)=minn≥1⁡{a/n+(n−1)/2}.g(a)=\min_{n\geq 1}\left\{a/n+(n-1)/2\right\}.

The following elementary potential is the only scalar batching fact needed in the service analysis. We include its proof so that the two-site certificate is independent of any scalar or aggregation model.

Lemma 7.2 (Bounded queue potential).

For a>0a>0, choose an integer N≥1N\geq 1 with N⁡(N−1)/2≤a≤N⁡(N+1)/2N(N-1)/2\leq a\leq N(N+1)/2. Then g⁡(a)=a/N+(N−1)/2g(a)=a/N+(N-1)/2 and N−1≤g⁡(a)≤NN-1\leq g(a)\leq N. The function

ha​(n)={n​g​(a)−n⁡(n−1)/2,0≤n≤N,a,n≥Nh_{a}(n)=\begin{cases}ng(a)-n(n-1)/2,&0\leq n\leq N,\\ a,&n\geq N\end{cases}

is nondecreasing, satisfies ha​(0)=0h_{a}(0)=0 and 0≤ha​(n)≤a0\leq h_{a}(n)\leq a, and obeys

n+ha​(n+1)−ha​(n)≥g⁡(a)(n≥0).n+h_{a}(n+1)-h_{a}(n)\geq g(a)\qquad(n\geq 0).

Consecutive terms a/n+(n−1)/2a/n+(n-1)/2 in the definition of gg differ by 1/2−a/[n⁡(n+1)]1/2-a/[n(n+1)]. Thus NN is a minimizer and the stated bounds on g⁡(a)g(a) follow from the inequalities defining NN. The two formulas for hah_{a} agree at NN. For n<Nn<N, its increment is g⁡(a)−n≥0g(a)-n\geq 0, and n+ha​(n+1)−ha​(n)=g⁡(a)n+h_{a}(n+1)-h_{a}(n)=g(a). For n≥Nn\geq N, the increment is zero and n≥N≥g⁡(a)n\geq N\geq g(a). This proves all assertions, including at a common endpoint where either adjacent choice of NN is valid. ∎

This potential supplies the following two-sided Poisson lower certificate.

Lemma 7.3.

Suppose the two endpoints receive independent Poisson streams of the same rate μ>0\mu>0, their distance is w>0w>0, and requests have waiting coefficient ρ>0\rho>0. For either prescribed initial endpoint and every T≥0T\geq 0,

𝔼⁡[OPTTtwo]≥ρ4​g​(μ​w/ρ)​T.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}^{\rm two}_{T}]\geq\frac{\rho}{4}g(\mu w/\rho)T.
Proof.

Apply Lemma 7.2 to the threshold policy, with a=μ​w/ρa=\mu w/\rho. If nn requests wait opposite the server, put V⁡(n)=(ρ/μ)​ha​(n)V(n)=(\rho/\mu)h_{a}(n). ρ​n+μ⁡[V⁡(n+1)−V⁡(n)]≥ρ​g​(a).\rho n+\mu[V(n+1)-V(n)]\geq\rho g(a).

Boundedness of VV and the finite expected number of arrivals justify the expectation.

Every crossing clears the opposite queue, lowers its potential to zero, and costs w≥V⁡(n)w\geq V(n). Starting from V⁡(0)=0V(0)=0, telescoping the arrival increments and crossing decreases therefore gives

𝔼⁡[movement and waiting through ​T]+𝔼⁡[V⁡(nT)]≥ρ​g​(a)​T.\mathbb{E}[\text{movement and waiting through }T]+\mathbb{E}[V(n_{T})]\geq\rho g(a)T.

Thus the full completed cost satisfies 𝔼⁡[ALGTthreshold]≥ρ​g​(a)​T\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}^{\rm threshold}_{T}]\geq\rho g(a)T. Lemma 7.1 then yields 4​𝔼​[OPTTtwo]≥𝔼⁡[ALGTthreshold]4\,\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}^{\rm two}_{T}]\geq\,\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}^{\rm threshold}_{T}]. ∎

7.3 A fixed-home algorithm and its expected cost

The two-site analysis leaves two choices to make on a tree: where should the home be, and how frequently should each vertex be visited? We first choose the home so that no branch can contain most of the demand. We then extend the purchase/waiting balance along each root path, choosing periods that allow nearby visits to share their travel.

Choosing the home.

With no positive-rate sites, do nothing. With exactly one, move there on its first request and stay; this is optimal on every finite input. Henceforth assume at least two distinct vertices have positive rates. Choosing the vertex of highest individual rate need not work. Many lower-rate vertices may form a distant cluster whose combined demand is much larger; returning from that cluster to the highest-rate vertex would be unnecessarily expensive. Section 7.6 gives a quantitative example.

Instead, retain the minimal subtree spanning the positive-rate vertices, with physical weight WW, and let L=∑vλvL=\sum_{v}\lambda_{v}. Choose a rate-weighted centroid hh: every component left after deleting hh has rate at most L/2L/2. Thus each branch has at least as much arrival rate outside it as inside, as needed for the two-stream lower bound. Such a vertex exists: whenever one component has more than half the rate, move into it; the reverse direction then has less than half, so this walk cannot return along an edge and must terminate.

Choosing the periods.

Root the retained subtree at hh, let we=2​ℓew_{e}=2\ell_{e} be the round-trip cost of edge ee, and let Λv\Lambda_{v} be the rate below vertex vv. We use a continuous service scale qvq_{v} before rounding it to a period. Suppose the parent’s scale quq_{u} is already chosen. Across edge u​vuv, the sparse-demand choice increases this scale by at most wu​vw_{uv}. For frequent demand, we instead balance the edge cost with the increase in the quadratic waiting expression: the new scale qvq_{v} solves Λv​(qv2−qu2)/2=wu​v\Lambda_{v}(q_{v}^{2}-q_{u}^{2})/2=w_{uv}. Taking the smaller of these two choices gives

qh=0,qv=min⁡{qu+wu​v,qu2+2​wu​vΛv},pv=2θ+⌈log2⁡(qv/(2​ln⁡2))−θ⌉,q_{h}=0,\qquad q_{v}=\min\left\{q_{u}+w_{uv},\sqrt{q_{u}^{2}+\frac{2w_{uv}}{\Lambda_{v}}}\right\},\qquad p_{v}=2^{\theta+\lceil\log_{2}(q_{v}/(2\ln 2))-\theta\rceil}, (14)

where uu is the parent of vv and the common phase θ\theta is selected below. Zero-rate outer branches have been removed, so Λv>0\Lambda_{v}>0. Lemma 7.4 will show how these local balances add up to the cost of the tours.

The values qvq_{v} increase along root paths. Rounding the scaled values qv/(2​ln⁡2)q_{v}/(2\ln 2) with a common phase makes each descendant period an integer multiple of every nonroot ancestor period. We use a common time unit and origin, so a descendant’s tick is also a tick of its nonroot ancestors. At a tick we take the union of paths to due vertices with pending requests and make one closed tour of that subtree. Shared edges are paid only once in each direction, and any other pending requests encountered are served as well.

Figure 2 illustrates the edge-sharing purpose of the common time origin. A due request at a descendant can make the tour traverse its whole root path, and a due request at an ancestor is cleared on that same tour. The algorithm computes the union of paths before moving, so it never pays separately for their overlap.

Every request is served by its next own tick, or earlier on another tour. Finite periods therefore complete every finite input without an end signal. The initial move costs at most d⁡(s0,h)d(s_{0},h), already included in the bound below.

Write B=∑v≠hλv​qvB=\sum_{v\neq h}\lambda_{v}q_{v}. We choose the common phase using the rates and lengths before execution. Its analysis also accounts for every final clearing.

Lemma 7.4 (Clock balance).

For an edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) oriented away from hh, write x=qux=q_{u}, y=qvy=q_{v}, Δ=y−x\Delta=y-x, w=wew=w_{e}, and Λ=Λv\Lambda=\Lambda_{v}. Then 0<Δ≤w0<\Delta\leq w and

wΔ=max⁡{1,Λ⁡(x+y)/2},w​min⁡{Λ,1/y}≤Λ​Δ.\frac{w}{\Delta}=\max\{1,\Lambda(x+y)/2\},\qquad w\min\{\Lambda,1/y\}\leq\Lambda\Delta. (15)

∑v≠hΛv​(qv−qpar⁡(v))=∑v≠hλv​qv=B.\sum_{v\neq h}\Lambda_{v}(q_{v}-q_{\operatorname{par}(v)})=\sum_{v\neq h}\lambda_{v}q_{v}=B. (16)

Both candidates exceed xx. If y=x+wy=x+w, comparison with the square root gives Λ⁡(x+y)/2≤1\Lambda(x+y)/2\leq 1, and w​min⁡{Λ,1/y}≤w​Λ=Λ​Δw\min\{\Lambda,1/y\}\leq w\Lambda=\Lambda\Delta. 7.3.1 Choosing the common clock scale

Use the periods in (14) and put a0=1/(2​ln⁡2)a_{0}=1/(2\ln 2). Write

7.6 Why the choice of home matters

For two or more positive-rate sites, Algorithm 1 uses a fixed home after its initial relocation. Its guarantees compare with the unrestricted mobile optimum; they do not identify an optimal causal rate or an optimal home.

A failed home-selection rule.

Highest individual rate is insufficient when the number of points grows. For m≥2m\geq 2, put a site AA of rate 11 at zero, and mm sites of rate 1/21/2 in an interval of width ε=m−4\varepsilon=m^{-4} starting at L=m2L=m^{2}. Consider policies consisting of instantaneous closed excursions from AA, with the server at AA between excursions. Every excursion serving the cluster costs at least 2​L2L.

With cluster rate μ=m/2\mu=m/2, use blocks of half-length q=L/μq=\sqrt{L/\mu}. The one-sided certificate

min⁡(2​L,q​N),\min(2L,qN),

N∼Pois⁡(μ​q)N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\mu q), charges either an excursion in the block or the wait of its first-half arrivals when no excursion occurs. Different blocks use disjoint movements and request sets. For X=q​NX=qN, one has 𝔼⁡[X]=L\mathbb{E}[X]=L and 𝔼⁡[X2]≤2​L2\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]\leq 2L^{2}. Cauchy–Schwarz gives

𝔼⁡[min⁡{2​L,X}]≥(𝔼⁡[X])2𝔼⁡[X]+𝔼⁡[X2]/(2​L)≥L/2≥L/3.\mathbb{E}[\min\{2L,X\}]\geq\frac{(\mathbb{E}[X])^{2}}{\mathbb{E}[X]+\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]/(2L)}\geq L/2\geq L/3.

Thus any such home policy has rate at least

L​μ/6=Ω⁡(m3/2).\sqrt{L\mu}/6=\Omega(m^{3/2}).

A home at the near end of the cluster serves its interior by immediate round trips at rate at most m​εm\varepsilon, and visits AA with period 2​L2\sqrt{L}, costing rate at most 2​L=2​m2\sqrt{L}=2m.

The unique highest-rate home therefore loses Ω⁡(m)\Omega(\sqrt{m}) even against a causal comparator. A rate median or centroid avoids this example.

The example shows why the home should reflect the distribution of demand across the tree, rather than the rate at one vertex. Our centroid choice provides the outside streams needed by the lower bound. It remains interesting to improve the constants or extend the constant guarantee to general metrics without a tree-embedding loss. Another direction is to study how the policy can learn arrival rates from observed requests.

8 Conclusion

Known Poisson arrival rates allow fixed spatial choices to compete with an offline optimum that adapts to the realized demand. Demand radii and a space–time certificate justify a fixed facility assignment. Connected regions justify fixed roots on a tree, after which the local rooted-forest lemma supplies the temporal scheduler and the certificate used to select an assignment. A rate-weighted centroid and balanced cut projections justify returning a mobile server to one home, even though the optimum need never return. These are three complementary ways to control the cost of a spatial restriction, with complete finite-horizon comparisons in each case.

The multi-root construction also admits polynomial deterministic preprocessing through a local-marginal LP and a constructive support decomposition. The facility and mobile algorithms use finite real-arithmetic constructions; their exact algebraic computations carry no polynomial bit-complexity claim here. Improving the constants, making the root preprocessing practical, and extending the tree arguments to general metrics remain natural questions. Learning arrival rates from observations would require a further analysis: the present policies know the rates when they choose their assignments, home, and clocks.

Appendix A Connected terminal assignment

We specialize the growing connected 00-extension process of Englert et al. [7, Section 4, Algorithm 1] to the augmented tree. The growing assignment construction is due to their work. Here we use randomly shifted depth partitions, a finite mixture of quadrupling scales, and a joint endpoint analysis to derive the explicit service-projection constant 313/8313/8. We give the tree implementation and its analysis in full.

Let TT be a finite tree with positive edge lengths and terminal set K≠∅K\neq\varnothing. The assignment is chosen independently of requests, and the service bound holds for every fixed service. Zero-length edges are contracted as in the multi-root model.

A.1 The partition and its elementary properties

If no positive edge remains after contraction, the assertion is trivial. Let m>0m>0 be the shortest positive edge length. Fix a depth origin. At scale Δ\Delta, choose an independent uniform offset in [0,Δ/2)[0,\Delta/2) and delete edges meeting an offset depth level modulo Δ/2\Delta/2. Components are connected, have diameter at most Δ\Delta, and separate a fixed pair u,vu,v with probability at most

min⁡{2​dT​(u,v)/Δ,1}.\min\{2d_{T}(u,v)/\Delta,1\}.

Indeed an edge is cut with probability at most its length divided by Δ/2\Delta/2, and a union bound applies along the unique path. The diameter bound follows because a component lies in one depth slab of width Δ/2\Delta/2 and every path between its vertices stays in the component. Once Δ\Delta is at least the tree diameter, use the single whole-tree cluster instead.

Initially assign each terminal its own label. Choose JJ uniformly from {0,…,63}\{0,\ldots,63\} and use scales Δi=(m/2)​4i+J/64\Delta_{i}=(m/2)4^{i+J/64} for i=0,1,…i=0,1,\ldots, with a fresh independent partition at each round. Freeze the previously assigned vertices. In each cluster touching an assigned vertex, remove all frozen vertices, and assign each remaining connected component the label of one frozen neighbor, using a fixed tie rule. Other vertices remain unassigned. Assigned labels never change. The whole-tree round terminates the process.

Every fiber remains connected because a new component is attached to an existing vertex with the same label. With ρ=4/3\rho=4/3, a vertex first assigned in round ii has

dT​(v,f⁡(v))≤∑h=0iΔh<ρ​Δi.d_{T}(v,f(v))\leq\sum_{h=0}^{i}\Delta_{h}<\rho\Delta_{i}.

This follows by induction through the assigned neighbor in its cluster. If one endpoint of an uncut edge was assigned before a round, its other endpoint is assigned by the end of that round. If both endpoints were unassigned and the edge is uncut, they belong to the same remaining component, so any labels newly given to them are equal.

The offsets have a finite exact representation: sort vertex depth residues modulo Δ/2\Delta/2 and sample an open cell with probability proportional to its length. Its midpoint gives the identical edge partition. There are finitely many rounds and cells; no continuous sampling or limiting partition is required. The phase sampler below explains exact sampling of the finitely many algebraic cell probabilities.

Fix an edge of length ℓ\ell. If exactly one endpoint is assigned, the other remains unassigned after a later round only if that edge is cut in that round. Conditional on the previous history, this has probability at most

pj=min⁡{1,2​ℓ/Δj}.p_{j}=\min\{1,2\ell/\Delta_{j}\}.

Independent fresh offsets give products of these bounds across rounds. Define the two convergent positive series

S4=∑k=0∞4−k(k+1)/2,B4=2+∑n=1∞(8/3)n4−n(n+1)/2,H4=2(4+3S4).S_{4}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}4^{-k(k+1)/2},\qquad B_{4}=2+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(8/3)^{n}4^{-n(n+1)/2},\qquad H_{4}=2(4+3S_{4}).

A.4 A finite mixture of scales

The finite phase mixture gives the following uniform projection bound.

Theorem A.2.

For every finite edge-weighted tree and nonempty terminal set, there is a finitely supported distribution of connected terminal retractions such that, for every fixed connected service subtree SS containing a terminal and every client set A⊆V⁡(S)A\subseteq V(S),

𝔼f[∑r∈Kw(⋃x∈A:f⁡(x)=rPT(x,r))]≤3138w(S).\mathbb{E}_{f}\left[\sum_{r\in K}w\left(\bigcup_{x\in A:f(x)=r}P_{T}(x,r)\right)\right]\leq\frac{313}{8}w(S).

Consequently, for every fixed finite input,

𝔼f​[OPTf⁡(I)]≤3138​OPTfree⁡(I).\mathbb{E}_{f}[\operatorname{OPT}_{f}(I)]\leq\frac{313}{8}\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm free}(I).

The assignment is sampled once, independently of the input.

A.4.1 Finite sampling

Use the sampler defined at the start of this appendix. Its initial scale is less than 2​m2m, so every edge is cut in that round unless the whole-tree override already terminates the process. For rational edge lengths, scales and offset-cell probabilities are algebraic because 4J/64=2J/324^{J/64}=2^{J/32}. Fair bits sample them exactly: refine a binary uniform interval and certified cumulative-probability intervals until one cell is determined. With finitely many boundaries, the probability of needing more than nn bits is O⁡(2−n)O(2^{-n}); boundary equality is a null event. Thus the sampler has finite support and terminates almost surely, without a continuous phase limit.

A finite exact-arithmetic computation evaluates these enclosures on the grid 2−96​ℤ2^{-96}\mathbb{Z}. The endpoints involving 21/642^{1/64} are bracketed by integer 64th-power comparisons. Lower products are rounded down, and upper products and divisions are rounded up by integer quotient and remainder. No floating-point operation is used. 3099078927284629529722094560869296<3138.\frac{3099078927284629529722094560869}{2^{96}}<\frac{313}{8}.

A.4.5 Terminal edges and the service projection

If one endpoint is a terminal, the first-assignment radius is zero. The initial scale is below 2​m≤2​ℓ2m\leq 2\ell, so the same threshold calculation gives 𝔼⁡[ΔJ]≤H4​ℓ\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{J}]\leq H_{4}\ell for every phase. Thus 𝔼⁡[Wf​(e)]≤(1+ρ​H4)​ℓ<21.8​ℓ\mathbb{E}[W_{f}(e)]\leq(1+\rho H_{4})\ell<21.8\ell. If both endpoints are terminals, Wf​(e)=ℓW_{f}(e)=\ell. All edges therefore satisfy 𝔼⁡[Wf​(e)]≤(313/8)​ℓ\mathbb{E}[W_{f}(e)]\leq(313/8)\ell.

The deterministic conversion established above gives

∑r∈Kw(⋃x∈A:f⁡(x)=rPT(x,r))≤∑e∈E⁡(S)Wf(e).\sum_{r\in K}w\left(\bigcup_{x\in A:f(x)=r}P_{T}(x,r)\right)\leq\sum_{e\in E(S)}W_{f}(e).

Taking expectations proves the service bound. For an arbitrary fixed free-root schedule, split each batch by its assigned terminal and keep all service times unchanged. Spatial cost increases by at most 313/8313/8 in expectation, while additive waiting is unchanged. Taking the infimum over the original schedule proves Theorem A.2.
